raw_response.blind_rationale: Blind reading of the full text confirms that S358 (Williams et al., 2025) does not belong in SWiM Families A, B or C (`none_nonfit`) and warrants a Criterion 4 scope flag (`E04` hydrological/environmental resource state). First, although the authors use the label "access" in their conceptual "trivalent framework" to describe predictor variables (GMA Active Management Area vs Non-Designated Area status, Tribal vs State SDWA primacy, CWS vs exempt private Domestic Well Area status, and Census demographics), the actual dependent variable in the Abstract and all four regression tables (Tables 2, 3, A1 and A2) is physical subbasin aquifer water-level decline/change (`ft/year` from ADWR index wells over 2001–2020 and 2011–2020). Aquifer water-table depletion is an environmental water-resource quantity outcome (`E04`), not household or community drinking-water access, connection, coverage, service continuity or affordability. Second, groundwater level stability cannot even serve as a monotonic proxy for safe drinking-water access in this study because rising/stabilizing groundwater levels mobilize contaminants and significantly increase both arsenic and nitrate detection and MCL exceedances (`OR = 1.01` and `OR = 1.05`, `p < 0.001`, p. 15). Third, while Section 3.5 (p. 15) briefly mentions un-tabulated models predicting regulatory `MCLExceeded` from Non-Designated Area (`NDA`) status, no standard errors or CIs are reported, the dataset pools EPA CWS compliance samples with USGS/ADEQ private/ambient groundwater observations, and the effects run in opposite directions across contaminants (`OR = 1.11, p = 0.004` for arsenic vs `OR = 0.48, p < 0.001` for nitrate). Fourth, the paper exhibits severe internal statistical reporting anomalies: Table 2 mislabels exponentiated odds ratios `exp(est.)` as "Log Odds"; Table 3 models a continuous water-level response yet still exponentiates linear coefficients into astronomical "Log Odds" values (e.g. `6.27E+39` for arsenic and `3305.44` for Tribal primacy) with reversed signs relative to Table 2; and Tables A1–A2 copy the continuous-model coefficients from Table 3 while mislabeling the response footnote as a binary decline variable (`1 = decline`), with tiny standard errors indicating regressions were estimated at the water-sample level (`27,334` arsenic / `47,783` nitrate records) rather than across the `1,881` service areas without clustering adjustments documented. If an exposure-only classification were forced, GMA/SDWA regulatory oversight and CWS regulation would map closest to Family C (or Tribal sovereignty to Family A), but `none_nonfit` (and PI review under `E04`) is clearly required because no household/service access outcome is estimated.

raw_response.headline_estimate_summary: Primary tabulated models (Table 2, PDF p. 16) estimate multivariate logistic regressions of binary subbasin groundwater level (GWL) decline (1 = decline over 20 years [2001–2020] and 10 years [2011–2020]) on regulatory/policy and binary water-quality predictors (note: Table 2 mislabels the Odds Ratio column exp(est.) as 'Log Odds'): (1) SDWA Primacy (Tribal vs State): in the Arsenic model, 20-yr GWL decline est. = -0.484, SE = 0.008, Statistic = -57.086, p < 0.001, OR = 0.62 (Abstract headline); 10-yr est. = -0.367, SE = 0.009, Statistic = -40.059, p < 0.001, OR = 0.69; in the Nitrate model, 20-yr est. = -0.173, SE = 0.017, Statistic = -10.289, p < 0.001, OR = 0.84; 10-yr est. = -0.112, SE = 0.02, Statistic = -5.725, p < 0.001, OR = 0.89. (2) GMA Designation (Non-Designated Area [NDA] vs designated AMA/INA): in the Arsenic model, 20-yr GWL decline est. = 0.431, SE = 0.008, Statistic = 51.122, p < 0.001, OR = 1.54; 10-yr est. = 0.418, SE = 0.009, Statistic = 45.877, p < 0.001, OR = 1.52; in the Nitrate model, 20-yr est. = 0.300, SE = 0.007, Statistic = 43.109, p < 0.001, OR = 1.35; 10-yr est. = 0.178, SE = 0.008, Statistic = 22.100, p < 0.001, OR = 1.20. (3) Supply Type (unregulated Domestic Well Area [DWA] vs SDWA-regulated Community Water System [CWS]): Nitrate model 20-yr est. = 0.033, SE = 0.006, Statistic = 5.758, p < 0.001, OR = 1.03 (10-yr est. = 0.014, SE = 0.007, p = 0.029, OR = 1.01); Arsenic model 20-yr est. = 0.014, SE = 0.007, p = 0.058, OR = 1.01 (10-yr est. = -0.024, SE = 0.008, p = 0.003, OR = 0.98). Continuous GWL models (Table 3, PDF p. 17; Tables A1–A2, PDF pp. 25–26, controlling for aquifer type, contaminant concentration, demographics, housing and interactions) show reversed signs and improperly exponentiated linear coefficients (e.g. 20-yr NDA est. = -5.989 [SE = 0.286] and -10.46 [SE = 0.330], p < 0.001; Tribal Primacy est. = 6.621 [SE = 0.684] and 8.103 [SE = 0.330], p < 0.001; % Black est. = 0.698, SE = 0.03, p < 0.001, OR = 2.01). Secondary text-only estimates (Section 3.5, PDF p. 15, no SEs reported) regress MCL exceedance on NDA status: arsenic MCL exceedance Estimate = 0.101, p = 0.004, OR = 1.11; nitrate MCL exceedance Estimate = -0.733, p < 0.001, OR = 0.48.
raw_response.study_design_and_sample: Observational spatiotemporal ecological study in Arizona, USA, across N = 1,881 mapped groundwater-supplied drinking water service areas (55.3% SDWA-regulated Community Water Systems [CWS] and 44.7% unregulated private Domestic Well Areas [DWAs]), linked to ADWR subbasin index-well groundwater level change rates over 20-year (2001–2020) and 10-year (2011–2020) periods and 27,334 arsenic and 47,783 nitrate monitoring observations (1998–2019; 97.8% of arsenic and 54.5% of nitrate observations imputed below MDL). Standard errors in Tables 2, 3, A1 and A2 (e.g. SE = 0.006–0.009) indicate regressions were fit at the contaminant-observation level rather than N = 1,881 service areas.
